pr_title: ossl_dh_check_priv_key: Do not fail on private keys without q
pr_body:
Fixes #18098

##### Checklist
<!-- Remove items that do not apply. For completed items, change [ ] to [x]. -->
- [ ] tests are added or updated
pr_comments:
I'll add tests later.

@slontis An alternative would be to not call ossl_dh_check_priv_key from the provider if dh->q is NULL. Which one do you prefer?

Since the check is about a known safe prime, we can calculate Q.

But since the check should be about a known safe prime, and the bug report was about a generated safe prime, I don't understand why does this patch make a difference?

> Since the check is about a known safe prime, we can calculate Q.
> 
> But since the check should be about a known safe prime, and the bug report was about a generated safe prime, I don't understand why does this patch make a difference?

The function as a whole is NOT just about checking known safe primes. And it MUST NOT fail if the parameters are not a known safe prime. So we do not really know q.
There is a part of the code that is abou safe primes and that is changed.
Also, the function that is called does not support calling it with 2^N for a non-approved safe prime. So either we can calculate Q or need it.

I am sorry, Kurt, I do not understand what do you want. The function is called for any DH private keys and it will currently fail for those with no q. As the function should be general (it is not called ossl_dhx_or_known_safe_prime_check_priv_key) it MUST NOT fail on keys without q.

Or do you think the alternative as mentioned in my above comment addressed to Shane is better? Then the function should be documented that it won't work on keys without q and it must never be called from other places if q is not present.

We're calling the ossl_ffc_validate_private_key() function. That function is documented as:
`
See SP800-56Ar3 Section 5.6.2.1.2: Owner assurance of Private key validity.
Verifies priv_key is in the range [1..upper-1]. The passed in value of upper
is normally params->q but can be 2^N for approved safe prime groups.
Note: This assumes that the domain parameters are valid.
`

This change breaks the condition in which the function produces correct output, because you pass 2^N for something that is not an `approved safe prime`.

As far as I know, all DH keys we have in the source are safe primes. If it's a safe prime, you can calculate Q.

If it's not a safe prime, as far as I know, you still need to know Q to be able to do the check.

I think it's wrong for this function to just skip the check if Q is not present and say everything is OK. Either it needs to return that it can't check it, or it should not have been called.

The code seems to assume that if DH_get_nid() says it knows it that it's an `approved safe prime`. I doubt that all the keys we internally have are approved safe primes. I also wonder if an application can add it's own primes to the list. It at least looks more sane to never use the 2^N.
Kurt, the key is not broken, the EVP_PKEY_check() on it should not fail. What is your alternative proposal, how to handle it.

My requirements:
- If you can't tell it's broken or not, don't claim everything is ok and return 1.
- Don't call ossl_ffc_validate_private_key() with invalid parameters

So there are several options which you can go with:
- This is expected behaviour, calling that function without Q is an error.
- If Q is not present, and it's a safe prime calculate Q.
- If Q is not present, and you don't know if it's a safe prime, check that it's a safe prime. This might be more expensive than what we want to do, but since you're checking the private key, it means you don't trust the private key and probably shouldn't trust the prime either.
- Change the code so it can indicate it's not checked. This is probably an API change. We document -2 as algorithm not supported which doesn't really match, and let the calling code deal with how to handle it.
- If you know you can't check it, don't check it.

I'm not sure we have a format in which we can save Q, making it more difficult to use non-standard primes. But you should probably avoid them in the first place.

Breaking the API is clearly a no-go.

Failing EVP_PKEY_check() on keys we generated is clearly a bug.

Checking whether a p is a safe prime would be possible, however that is a little bit expensive check, not sure it is a good idea to do it.

Also please look at how we generate the keys in the case q == NULL. We should not fail private key check on keys we generated. And another thing - see how the ossl_dh_check_priv_key is called from the providers. It should really be a quick sanity check of the private key and not include checking whether the parameters are sane, there are other calls for that.

My suggestion is then to not call ossl_ffc_validate_private_key() in case Q is not present, and also use `l = dh->length ? dh->length : BN_num_bits(dh->params.p) - 1` and check that it's in that range.
Note that the dh->length might be present in the file. I'm not sure if we save that or not.
The intention of the function was to fail if there is no q.. In terms of a 'proper' key check that is what it should do... A private key without a 'q' cannot really be deemed to be valid..
Then why does the openssl library/command line utility generate such keys?

> The intention of the function was to fail if there is no q.. In terms of a 'proper' key check that is what it should do... A private key without a 'q' cannot really be deemed to be valid..

@slontis, that's a nonsense. Why should it be? If the p is a safe-prime, storing the q is just redundant.

The case where q is missing is not (always) for the case where p is a safe prime, see for instance PKCS#3 and RFC 2631. The private key check should match the range we use for generating such keys. I think what we implement in case of a missing q is PKCS#3, so the check should probably be 2^(l-1) ≤ x < 2^l.

We should probably deprecate PKCS#3.

> > The intention of the function was to fail if there is no q.. In terms of a 'proper' key check that is what it should do... A private key without a 'q' cannot really be deemed to be valid..
> 
> @slontis, that's a nonsense. Why should it be? If the p is a safe-prime, storing the q is just redundant.

I was not talking about the case where q can be regenerated, I am talking about the other 'types' such as fips186-4/2.

> We should probably deprecate PKCS#3.

This will be difficult for <= TLSv1.2. The DH implementation there does not transmit the "q" value.

> This will be difficult for <= TLSv1.2. The DH implementation there does not transmit the "q" value.

If they send a known prime, we internally do know q, and afaik, use it.

> If they send a known prime, we internally do know q, and afaik, use it.

But they are not required to send a known prime and I do not think we should break connections with such peers. Anyway this is IMO off topic.
ping for the second review

> It needs more tests.

I am not going to spend more time on artificial test cases for this, I am sorry. This is really not good use of my time. Anybody who likes to can add more testcases later.

@slontis please reapprove
also ping for second review
Sorry @t8m don't think I'm competent enough :(

I think the code change is fine, but would have written things
differently.

I think this PR should have more tests to comply with our testing policy.
This pull request is ready to merge
Merged to master and 3.0 branches. Thank you for the reviews.

comments:
Hi david,
I would suggest reading doc/man7/EVP_PKEY-DH.pod to get an idea of some of the problems related to validation of DH/DSA keys.
I also suggest that moving towards using named safe primes groups is probably a good idea.
For backward compatability reasons if you specifiy the algorithm as DH (or DHX) it uses an older style generator or (FIPS186-2 related params) with your above commands in the default provider..
If you use DHX as the algorithm it at least saves out Q (but by default it then uses FIPS186-2). FOR FIPS186-4/2 Doing a proper key check involves using all the parameters used for the key generation (some of which are not saved in the output key even when using DHX). Because of all these issues moving towards using safe prime groups is recommended.
(I am not suggesting @t8m should not address the issue - just trying to explain what is going on)

review_comments: I think we can assume that p exists.
I think upper ends up as an uninitialized variable here.
Shouldn't we init dh->length in this case?

FIPS should care about the fips186-4 and named group types.. For both these cases q needs to be set. If you want to do this code I suggest leaving the code how it was for fips mode.. i.e return an error if q is NULL.
 For FIPS 186-4 If someone loads a key and doesnt set the q, seed and counter themselves then the validation MUST FAIL.

For the non fips case it may need to be more flexible. Although arguably FIPS 186-2 should also fail if it doesnt have these values set either.
Have you read the patch, Shane? It does not change anything when FIPS_MODULE is defined.
This test requires either (dh->params.p != NULL || dh->length != 0)
A DH key without p can never be valid.
